org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Source: `request.getQueryString()` (attacker-controlled query string). The value is extracted into `param` (substring around the `BenchmarkTest02556=` marker, trimmed at `&`) at lines ~55-68, then passed through `java.net.URLDecoder.decode(param, "UTF-8")`. It is then handed to the project helper `BenchmarkTest02556.doSomething(request, param)`, whose body shows `int num = 196; if ((500/42)+num > 200) bar = param; else bar = "..."` — the condition (511 > 200) is always true, so `bar` is returned as the raw, unmodified tainted `param`. `bar` then flows directly into the flagged sink `java.io.File fileTarget = new java.io.File(bar);` (line 72) and immediately into `fileTarget.exists()`. No sanitizer adequate for a path sink is on the path: `URLDecoder.decode` only performs URL decoding (it does not strip `../` or restrict to a base directory), and the only other call, `ESAPI.encoder().encodeForHTML(fileTarget.toString())`, is applied AFTER the File object is constructed and only encodes the string for HTML output — it does not sanitize the path used by `new File(...)`. Thus fully attacker-controlled path data (including `../` sequences) reaches the filesystem API unchecked.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The servlet takes a raw query-string parameter, URL-decodes it, passes it unchanged through the `doSomething` helper, and uses it directly as the path argument to `new java.io.File(bar)` with no canonicalization, base-directory restriction, or `FilenameUtils.getName`-style sanitization. The taint reaches the filesystem API intact and the `fileTarget.exists()` call gives an attacker-dependent observable result.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: An attacker controls the file path used by the application, enabling path traversal to arbitrary locations on the server. Although this specific test code only calls `fileTarget.exists()`, it exposes a file/directory existence oracle (allowing enumeration of server filesystem contents and probing of sentinel files); in realistic variants where the same tainted path is used for read/write/open, this becomes arbitrary file access.
remediation: Do not use client-supplied data directly as a file path; map user input to a server-side identifier (whitelist) and resolve the real path from a fixed base directory.
If a filename must be accepted, sanitize with `org.apache.commons.io.FilenameUtils.getName(...)` and reject any input containing `..`, path separators, or absolute-path prefixes.
Resolve the canonical path and verify it is contained within the intended base directory (e.g. `file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(baseDir + File.separator)`) before any file operation.

Depending on how the invoked script consumes the value, this can lead to OS command execution / remote code execution on the host, or at minimum attacker-controlled environment for the child process.
remediation: Do not pass user-supplied data into Runtime.exec()/ProcessBuilder; use a fixed command with no user input.
If user input is unavoidable, validate it against a strict allow-list of permitted values and reject anything else before it reaches exec.

Never rely on URL-decoding or HTML encoding as protection for OS-command sinks; if a process must be spawned, pass arguments explicitly via ProcessBuilder (no shell) and avoid injecting the value into the environment or command line.

org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.exploitability_evidence: Traced the value that reaches the sink: in doPost, `String param = scr.getTheValue("BenchmarkTest02697")`. The body of SeparateClassRequest.getTheValue (shown under Called project methods) is `return "bar";` — a hardcoded string literal, NOT `request.getParameter(...)`. `param` (= "bar") is passed to doSomething, which only puts it into map29916 under "keyB-29916" and reads it back (`bar = (String) map29916.get("keyB-29916")`), returning the same constant "bar". In doPost, `argList.add("echo " + bar)` therefore produces the fixed literal "echo bar", which is passed to `pb.command(argList)` and `pb.start()`. There is no attacker-controlled source on the path — the HttpServletRequest is never read for the value (no getParameter/getHeader/etc. flows into the sink), so no taint (let alone a sanitization gap) exists to be exploited. The scanner matched the string-concatenation-into-ProcessBuilder pattern while the operand originates from a constant.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.root_cause: The flag is a pattern match on `"echo " + bar` fed to ProcessBuilder, but `bar` resolves to the hardcoded constant "bar" (via SeparateClassRequest.getTheValue -> doSomething -> map get). The value reaching the sink is a compile-time constant, not user input, so the CWE-78 taint condition is not met.
org/owasp/benchmark/testcode/BenchmarkTe.impact: No security impact: the executed command is the fixed string `sh -c "echo bar"` (or `cmd.exe /c "echo bar"` on Windows); a user cannot influence it, so no OS command injection is possible.
remediation: No code change required for this instance; it is a benign constant-derived command.

If this helper was intended to expose a request value, replace `return "bar";` with `return request.getParameter(parameter);` and then treat the sink as a real command-injection risk: never build a shell command by string concatenation.
Prefer passing arguments as separate ProcessBuilder list elements without a shell (`sh -c`/`cmd /c`), or use a fixed allow-list of commands and validate/escape any dynamic operand.
